summary: Deep technical review of quantization approaches for Tessera Bio's inference workloads. Discussed INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs, accuracy regressions observed on domain-specific prompts, KV cache warmup and batching impact on latency, and requirements for VPC/on-prem deployment. topics: INT8 vs FP8 vs GPTQ vs AWQ
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Amir (Redwood), Dr. Miguel Alvarez (Tessera), Sabrina Chen (Tessera infra), Liam O'Connor (CTO), Hannah Park (ML Research)

Summary (auto): quick high-level then deep dive on quantization.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, with Priya and Amir, and we'll do a technical deep dive into quantization tradeoffs for the models you're running.
00:12 Miguel: Great, thanks. We're mainly worried about accuracy drift for our assay-qa prompts when we go to 8-bit and the latency on-prem.
00:18 Priya: Yeah totally. Can you remind us of the model you currently run and the hardware?
00:24 Sabrina: We're on an internal fork of a 13B model — basically llama2-derived with biomedical fine-tuning — running on a mix of A100s and some 80GB cards. For on-prem pilot we'll likely use two A100-80GB nodes.
00:40 Amir: Got it. And what's your token distribution? Short prompts? Long prefixes?
00:45 Hannah: Mostly long prefixes, 300-800 tokens typical, and we do a lot of prefix-heavy retrieval augmentation where the KV cache is basically huge.
00:56 Priya: That matters a lot for quantization because KV cache footprint and precision can drive both latency and accuracy. Quick outline: we'll cover static INT8, FP8-ish approaches, GPTQ and AWQ post-training quantization, then discuss per-layer outliers and calibration strategies, and finally batching/KV cache effects for on-prem.
01:12 Liam: Sounds good. One quick item — from a security standpoint we need KMS integration and HSM, and SOC2 controls. We'll need that for the pilot.
01:22 Jordan: Yep we'll include security pack docs.

01:28 Priya: Starting with INT8 — classic 8-bit integer quantization. Pros: predictable memory/throughput wins, works well with quant-friendly kernels on our runtime. Cons: per-token quality drop can be noticeable for outlier layers, and you often need per-channel scaling or per-tensor calibration to avoid regressions on rare tokens.
01:50 Miguel: We've seen hallucinations increase on a handful of domain prompts when we tried a naive 8-bit conversion.
01:57 Priya: Right, that's expected. GPTQ and AWQ both try to preserve accuracy by handling weight distribution and outliers better. GPTQ does per-channel second-order error compensation via Hessian approximation — tends to be stronger on deep MLP layers. AWQ focuses on asymmetric weight quantization with per-block scales which can be better for attention layers.
02:17 Hannah: Do you have simple rules of thumb which to try first?
02:20 Priya: If you're latency-limited and want a fast path, INT8 with per-channel scales + outlier folding is a good starting point. If accuracy is critical on those biospec prompts, run GPTQ and AWQ both — they often have complementary strengths. In our benchmarks GPTQ kept accuracy within ~0.5-1.2% on most tasks, AWQ sometimes edges out GPTQ on attention-heavy recency tasks.
02:42 Amir: I can add that our runtime picks kernels based on quant format — AWQ and GPTQ sometimes require different microkernels; we can pick the best path automatically but on-prem GPUs need the right CUDA/cuBLAS versions.
02:56 Sabrina: That's a practical issue — our on-prem stack is slightly older on the driver side.
03:00 Priya: We can run a micro-benchmark to confirm which kernels are fastest on your stack.
03:06 Miguel: About FP8 — is that worth considering?
03:09 Priya: FP8 (bfloat-like or e5 variants) can give accuracy closer to FP16 with less quantization engineering but requires hardware/driver support and may not be available on all GPUs or runtimes. On A100 you can get some FP8 benefits with the right software, but for portability GPTQ/AWQ 8-bit paths are more mainstream.
03:28 Jordan: Also FP8 end-to-end may have less model conversion friction but higher fragility in mixed precision kernels.

03:35 Priya: Now accuracy regressions — common sources: outlier tokens/activations, layerwise scale mismatch, attention softmax sensitivity, and KV cache accumulation when using reduced precision for keys/values. We often see small but systematic token-level shifts that compound for long prefixes.
03:52 Hannah: Is there a way to keep the KV cache in higher precision while quantizing other weights?
03:56 Priya: Yes, hybrid strategies are common: keep KV cache (or attention keys/values) in FP16 while quantizing MLP weights to 8-bit. That mitigates long-prefix drift but costs memory. Another option is quantizing the model but decompressing KV cache entries on the fly — tradeoff between CPU/GPU cycles and memory.
04:14 Miguel: How big is the latency penalty for decompressing KV entries?
04:18 Amir: It depends on throughput and batch size. For single-stream low-latency, the penalty can be a few milliseconds; for high throughput batched workloads it's amortized. We'll measure on your hardware.

04:30 Priya: On batching — Redwood's continuous batching helps improve throughput but can increase tail latency if you have strict single-request SLOs. For your use case with long prefixes, larger batches help because KV cache reuse reduces per-token compute. But you told us latency SLO is 200-300ms P95?
04:47 Liam: Correct, 200-300ms P95 for interactive inference is the goal.
04:51 Priya: Okay. With GPTQ or AWQ on two A100-80GBs and hybrid KV precision, we think P95 is achievable for many prompt sizes, but we need to validate with real traffic shape. Micro-benchmarks will give us tokens/sec and P95 estimates.
05:05 Miguel: What about caching warm-up — first request cold-start is bad for us.
05:09 Priya: Right, cold-start for the KV cache makes the first few requests slower until the KV entries are populated. Strategies: pre-warming common prefixes, saving/restoring KV cache snapshots, or using a warm-up proxy that primes the cache. For on-prem, we can implement snapshot restore as part of deployment to reduce cold-start.
05:27 Sabrina: For our workflows we have a set of canonical prefixes — pre-warm seems easy.

05:33 Priya: Let's talk numbers: in our internal benchmark on a domain-adapted 13B model, turning on GPTQ reduced memory by ~2.8x and gave 1.8x-2.4x throughput increase, with end-task accuracy within 1% for most tasks. AWQ showed similar memory gains but sometimes slightly better on attention-dominant tests. INT8 baseline naive conversion had larger accuracy deltas up to 3-5% on edge prompts.
05:58 Miguel: That's in line with our experiments. Any tips for calibration datasets?
06:03 Priya: Use a calibration set that's as close as possible to your production distribution — including rare tokens and long context examples. Calibration should include temperature/decoding settings you use in prod. Also check for per-layer outliers and consider clipping or outlier folding for problematic layers.
06:22 Hannah: Are there automation tools to detect layers that matter most?
06:26 Priya: Yes — we run sensitivity analysis: quantize one layer at a time and measure deltas on a small eval to rank them. Then apply higher precision to top-k sensitive layers. We can run that sensitivity pass as part of the GPTQ job.

06:36 Amir: On the runtime side, we need to ensure kernel compatibility for AWQ/GPTQ on your driver. Sabrina, can you confirm if your cluster has CUDA 12.x or just 11.8?
06:45 Sabrina: We're on 11.8 at the moment. Upgrading to 12 is possible but takes a change window.
06:50 Amir: Some AWQ optimized kernels rely on newer CUDA primitives — if upgrade is not possible we'll fallback to alternate kernels which may be slightly slower but still workable. We'll capture that in the benchmark.

07:00 Miguel: For private deployments, network isolation is a must — VPC peering, private control plane are needed. Also KMS for keying.
07:09 Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPC and KMS integrations; for HSM we work with our infra team to validate the HSM provider. We'll include that in the security pack.
07:17 Liam: Audit logs and RBAC are mandatory.
07:20 Jordan: Yep, we have audit logs and SSO/SAML support; we'll share the SOC2/ISO excerpts.

07:26 Priya: Back to quantization regressions: sometimes token-level errors are in decoding — greedy vs sampling can amplify small differences. So for your eval, keep the same decoding config as prod. Also include reranking/LLM-chain steps if you apply them, since regressions can cascade.
07:45 Hannah: Good point, our pipeline does a clausify + rerank stage.

07:50 Priya: On measurement: we'll produce per-prompt accuracy delta, latency P50/P95, peak memory, and token/sec. We'll also show confusion cases where AWQ or GPTQ diverge. Expect a table like: prompt_id, baseline_score, gptq_score, awq_score, delta_gptq, delta_awq, latency_gptq_ms, latency_awq_ms.
08:11 Miguel: That will help the product team decide tradeoffs.

08:14 Priya: About model variants and fallback: if a quantized variant fails a regression threshold we advise fallbacks to FP16 for critical routes. Redwood runtime supports routing by policy — you can set a per-route accuracy SLO and fallback to FP16 or higher precision model.
08:29 Jordan: And we can also do canarying — route 5% traffic to quantized model and measure regressions in the wild.
08:36 Miguel: How long does an in-house GPTQ job run for a 13B model on two A100-80GBs?
08:42 Priya: Depends on optimization and dataset size. For a 10k calibration/eval set, expect 2-6 hours for full sensitivity + quantization with checkpointing. AWQ might be similar or faster depending on implementation. We'll provide exact estimates after we see your data and hardware.
08:59 Sabrina: Good to know. Also we want to understand how to restore a model if quantized variant shows issues.
09:05 Priya: We always keep the FP16 baseline and version it. Deployment can be atomic so you can revert quickly. We'll walk through the rollback steps in the pilot runbook.

09:12 Miguel: Any gotchas with tokenizer differences? We had some tokens split differently after a rebuild.
09:16 Priya: Tokenization mismatches are a frequent root cause of apparent accuracy regressions — ensure identical tokenizer, merges, and BPE vocab. We'll verify that in the pipeline.
09:25 Hannah: For the micro-benchmark, what telemetry will you need?
09:28 Amir: We'll need sample prompts, expected decoding settings, and the model checkpoint. Ideally SSH to a test node for direct runs, or we run on a mirrored env. Sabrina, you said you can provide a test node?
09:40 Sabrina: Yes, I'll share access details and an inference YAML by Friday.
09:44 Priya: Perfect. We'll also need an eval set with ground truth to compute accuracy deltas.
09:49 Miguel: We'll prepare a 10k eval set including long-prefix negative cases.

09:55 Jordan: Quick recap and next steps — Priya will run GPTQ vs AWQ on your eval set and share results; Jordan sends pricing and security docs; Sabrina shares infra spec. We'll schedule pilot kickoff after results. Anything else?
10:10 Liam: No, that's it. Thanks.
10:12 Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the benchmark sheet and the runbook.

(end of recording)
